questions.question: What distinguishes a composite benchmark from an evaluation dashboard?
options: A composite benchmark applies an explicit rule that combines component evidence, while a dashboard may preserve dimensions without one universal score
A dashboard always contains fewer tasks
A composite benchmark never shows component results
A dashboard cannot compare models
questions.explanation: Aggregation is a policy choice. A dashboard can expose trade-offs without claiming that one scalar is sufficient.

questions.question: A higher-is-better metric has a baseline of 20, a reference of 100, and an observed value of 60. What is its baseline-to-reference normalized score?
questions.explanation: The normalized score is (60 - 20) / (100 - 20) = 0.5, or 50 on a 0-100 scale.

questions.question: Why is averaging raw accuracy percentages with latency in milliseconds invalid?
options: The units and favorable directions differ, so the result is dominated by an arbitrary scale
Latency cannot be measured
Accuracy is always more important
Arithmetic means require exactly three components
questions.explanation: Metrics must share an interpretable direction and scale before weights can express policy rather than unit size.

questions.question: When is a geometric mean more informative than an arithmetic mean?
options: When normalized positive components should be non-compensatory enough that one weak result pulls the score down strongly
When negative values should increase the score
When missing components should be hidden
When every component must be ignored except the best
questions.explanation: A geometric mean penalizes imbalance more strongly. Its assumptions and treatment of zero must be documented.

questions.question: What is the main risk of adding three highly correlated reasoning tests?
options: The same capability may receive repeated influence while apparent coverage grows
All confidence intervals become zero
The benchmark can no longer be versioned
Every task receives equal weight automatically
questions.explanation: Task count is not independent evidence count. Correlation and shared provenance can make a portfolio look broader than it is.

questions.question: Two candidates swap rank after a small predeclared weight change. What is the defensible report?
options: The ordering is weight-sensitive, so preserve component results and avoid a definitive winner claim
Choose the result with more decimal places
Hide the alternative weights
Increase both scores by the same amount
questions.explanation: A fragile ranking says more about the aggregation policy than a stable capability difference.

questions.question: A release candidate has the highest composite average but fails a predeclared safety floor. What should happen?
options: Block or limit the release because unrelated strengths cannot cancel a hard requirement
Release because the average is highest
Lower the safety floor after seeing the result
Remove the safety component
questions.explanation: Hard gates represent requirements that are not exchangeable with other capabilities.

questions.question: Which record is necessary to reproduce a composite result after the benchmark evolves?
options: Versioned task data, runner and scorer versions, raw component results, normalization, weights, aggregation, missing-value policy, and exclusions
Only the final rank
Only the model name
A screenshot of the leaderboard
questions.explanation: A scalar without its evidence and policy cannot be recomputed, audited, or compared across versions.
